full_judgment:
7. In this second appeal the question of non joinder or misjoinder of necessary parties in the suit has not been pressed by the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant. The submissions made by the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant centered mainly round the question as to whether the under raiyati interests recorded in C.S. Khatian Nos. 848 and 847 are valid in law and whether the plaintiff is entitled to get a decree for ejectment of the under raiyats. It appears from the judgments of the Courts below that it was argued on behalf of the defendants that the under raiyati interests recorded in C.S. Khatian Nos. 848 and 847 and also 944 had been created before the Bengal Tenancy Act was amended in 1928 by which section 48F was incorporated along with some other sections and section 85 was omitted. Since section 48F is not applicable to the above mentioned under raiyati interest should be treated as valid in law and as such the undo raiyats cannot be treated as unauthorised trespassers in the suit land. In support of this contention reliance was placed on a decision of the Calcutta High Court, namely, Munshi Serajnl Huq Mia Vs. Abjal Mia and another reported in A.I.R. 1941 Cal. 351 same decision has been reported in 45 Calcutta Weekly Notes page 339. It appears that above noted argument of the learned Advocate did not find favour. The learned District Judge held that before the amendment of the Act in 1928 an under raiyat could create a sublease but it would not be binding upon the landlord because the under raiyati interest is not transferable which was made transferable only under section 48F of the amended Act 1928 with the consent of the landlord, and as such the sub-leases created by Baharulla and others are not binding upon the plaintiff and since the plaintiff has auction purchased the under raiyati of first decree the sub-leases created in favour of the defendants and their predecessor-in-interest, have ceased to exist and the plaintiff is entitled to get khas possession of the land by removing the defendants therefrom. 

 8. It further appears from the judgments of the Court below that the material question involved in the case, namely, validity or other-wise of the sub-leases created by the under raiyats prior to 1928 has not been considered in its proper perspective in view of amendment of the relevant provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act by the Bengal Tenancy Act (Amendment) 1938. A sub-lease created by an under raiyat prior to 1928 which is continuing for more than 12 years can no longer be treated as void, inoperative and not binding upon the landlord or his successor-in-interest. Even if, section 85(3) since repealed is presumed to be applicable to under raiyati interest created prior to 1928, the under raiyati lease which is valid for 9 years after the introduction of the new provisions in the Bengal Tenancy Act, and if at that time the landlord failed to resume the land covered by the under raiyatis this will mean recognition of the transfer which might be unauthorised. The Courts below have not considered the question of ejectment of the defendants who have been in the suit land for more than 40 years and they have got their homestead thereon on proper application of the law as it stands after amendments. Section 48G provides that an under raiyat who immediately before the commencement of the Bengal Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1928 had by custom a right of occupancy in any land, shall have a right of occupancy in that land. In this case, the C. S. Khatians (Exhibits 6 series) show that the disputed under raiyatis were duly recorded with a note that provisions of sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 48G will be applicable to the under raiyati interest. Therefore the under raiyati interests recorded' in C.S. Khatian Nos. 848, 847 and 844 acquired the status of occupancy right. From the documentary evidence it appears that all the transfers were made prior to 1928 by registered instruments. Section 26C provides the manner of transfer and notices to landlord etc. This section inter alia provides that “…..registering officer shall not accept for registration any such instrument unless the sale price or where there is no sale price, the value of the holding or portion or share thereof transferred is stated therein and unless it is accompanied in the prescribed manner by— 

 9. A transfer made in accordance with the provisions of section 26C of the Bengal Tenancy Act and if the landlord does not take any exception to that it will be deemed that transfer has been made with the consent of the landlord. For the purpose of ejectment of such an under raiyat as provided in sub-section (3) of section 48G—the interest of an under raiyat who has a right of occupancy in his holding shall not be deemed to be a protected interest under clause (d) of section 160. However section 48C provides protection to an under raiyat who has been in possession of his land for continuous period of 12 years whether before or partly before and partly after the commencement of the Bengal Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1928 or has a homestead thereon. Similar protection has also been granted to such an under raiyat under section 160, clause (c) of the Bengal Tenancy Act which provides that— 

 10. There is another aspect in this case, in the sale deed dated 11th June, 1941 under which the plaintiff purchased the raiyati interest recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 840 at a jama Of Rs.23/- from Rahim Baksha and others the under raiyati interests recorded in C. S. Khatian Nos. 844, 847 and 848 have also been mentioned in the schedule thereof. This recital in the sale deed along with the C. S. Khatian prepared in the name of the under raiyats wherein it has been recorded that the provisions of sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 48G of the Bengal Tenancy Act would be applicable leave no scope for doubt that the under raiyatis had acquired the status of occupancy right. 

 11. In this connection the decision of a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Promoth Nath Sikdar Vs. Jitendra Nath Roy reported in 43 Calcutta Weekly Notes p. 1102 may be referred to. This decision is on all fours for the present case. After examining the effect of the repeal of section 85 of the Bengal Tenancy Act it has been held that a sub-lease was created before 1928 without the consent of the landlord did not enable the landlord either to take immediate possession of the land, or to treat the tenancy under him forfeited on the ground that the tenant having done an unwarranted act. The learned Judges explained that this right could be exercised under section 85 of the Act, but this right cannot be preserved after the repeal of the section itself, because, it must be presumed that as if the repealed provision never existed except as to transactions past and closed. The plaintiff in the present case brought the suit for ejectment on the basis of purchase in execution of the rent decree obtained against the under raiyat after the repeal of section 85 so advantage of section 85 could not be taken as the section itself was not in existence when the cause of action arose. It has been further held that a right of occupancy acquired by an under raiyat by custom is not protected under clause (d) of section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act but the interest of such under raiyat is protected under clause (c) of section 160 if there is dwelling house, etc. In this context another decision of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Munshi Serajul Huq Mia and others Vs. Abdul Mia and another reported in 45 Calcutta Weekly Notes p. 339 may be referred to. This decision also is fully applicable to the present case. In this decision it has been held that the principle that decree for eviction against lessee is binding on sub-lessee even if not made party to the suit does not apply to a tenancy created under the Bengal Tenancy Act. Section 48F does not apply where an under raiyati holding of the second degree was created before 1928. As the law stood before that an under raiyati holding was neither heritable nor transferable but there was an exception in the case of a sub-lease as power to sub-let was implied in the definition of an under raiyat as given in section 4 of the Act. This view has been taken following the decision in the case of Dwaska Mondal Vs. Nalinee Kanta reported in 1938 Calcutta 223. It has been further held that a sub-lessee from an under raiyati of this nature can be ejected only in accordance with section 48C of the Bengal Tenancy Act and not otherwise. 

 12. In view of what has been stated above, it leads me to the irresistible conclusion that the under raiyati interests of second and third degree in favour of the defendants which were created before the amendment of the Bengal Tenancy Act in 1928 cannot be ejected at the instance of the plaintiff who stepped into the shoes of the raiyats with notice of the existing under-raiyati interests of second and third degree under the said raiyati interest and her cause of action to bring the action in ejectment also accrued after repeal of section 85. The defendants having acquired the status of occupancy raiyats by operation of law, cannot be ejected by the plaintiff on the basis of his auction purchase of the superior under raiyati interest of Ashatulla Sarker and others because the rent decree obtained by the plaintiff was not binding upon the defendants. The Courts below totally misdirected themselves on this vital question and failed to decide the case on proper application of the law and consequently this has led to an erroneous decision.
